# Vatthugāthā (Cnd 1)

**ID:** Cnd 1
**Section:** Cūḷaniddesa (cnd)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-2
**Title (Pali):** Vatthugāthā
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0516m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vatthugāthā* ("Introductory Verses") serves as the prologue and narrative setting for the *Pārāyanavagga* (Sn 976–1031) [Holt et al. 2003; Wynne, Origin of Buddhist Meditation]. Comprising 56 verses, the text narrates the story of the brāhmaṇa Bāvarī sending his sixteen disciples to the Buddha in order to determine whether Gotama bears the thirty-two marks of a great man (*mahāpurisa*) [Norman 1983; Holt et al. 2003; Goldstone 1978]. Although modern canonical editions place the *Vatthugāthā* as the opening text of the *Cūḷaniddesa* (Cnd 1), the body of the *Cūḷaniddesa* offers no commentary or gloss upon these introductory stanzas, commenting only upon the subsequent question-and-answer poems of the *Pārāyanavagga* and the *Khaggavisāṇasutta* [Hazra 1994; Kingsbury 2002; Norman 1983]. Scholars infer from this complete omission that the *Vatthugāthā* was either composed after the compilation of the *Cūḷaniddesa* or had not yet been accepted as an authentic canonical component of the vagga [Norman 1983; Norman 1997-2001; Holt et al. 2003]. Metrically, the verses are composed in Śloka, with verse 995 in mixed Triṣṭubh [Norman 1997-2001]. Later commentary in the *Paramatthajotikā* (Pj II) does comment upon the verses, attributing their compilation to Ānanda [Norman 1983; Norman 1997-2001].

Within the Pali tradition, the text of Cnd 1 matches almost verbatim with the *Vatthugāthā* of the *Sutta Nipāta* (Snp 5.1 / PTS Snp 190, segments 0.4–56.5) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also identifies substantial internal text reuse with several Pali commentarial works, especially the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* (Paramatthajotikā II), *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, and *Sīlakkhandhavaggaṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, Sanskrit fragments preserving the narrative of Bāvarī, Kapilavastu, and the marks of a *mahāpurisa* parallel the subject matter of the text, though without exact verbal agreement [Norman 1997-2001]. Machine alignments computed by DharmaNexus further align portions of the text with Sanskrit Buddhist narratives, most notably the *Lalitavistara*, as well as Chinese Āgama literature (*Madhyama Āgama*, T 26) and Tibetan narrative anthologies [DharmaNexus].
